items: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 with Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 is the core law. CDSCO, headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), regulates new drugs, imports and clinical trials; states license manufacture and sale.
DTAB is the technical advisory body; DCC secures uniform administration across states; the Central Drugs Laboratory (Kolkata) is the appellate testing laboratory.
The Act separately defines misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs (and the same three for cosmetics). Know the clause-wise meaning of each; questions test the difference.
An Inspector taking a sample pays its fair price (unless waived), divides it into four portions, seals them, and sends one to the Government Analyst.

Schedule H: prescription-only drugs. Schedule H1: specified antibiotics, anti-TB and habit-forming drugs needing a separate register kept 3 years. Schedule X: narcotic and psychotropic drugs with stricter storage and records.

Schedule M: Good Manufacturing Practices (revised version notified December 2023). Schedule L-1: Good Laboratory Practices. Schedule P: life period of drugs. Schedule T: GMP for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs.

New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 replaced most of the old Schedule Y for clinical trials. Medical Devices Rules, 2017 classify devices by risk into A (low) to D (high). Cosmetics are now under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020.
NPPA (set up in 1997) fixes and monitors ceiling prices under DPCO 2013 for drugs in the National List of Essential Medicines.
Do not mix up Schedule H1 (antibiotics, anti-TB, habit-forming) with Schedule X (narcotic/psychotropic).
Questions often ask which body advises (DTAB) versus which coordinates states (DCC).
Spurious = imitation or substitute or false manufacturer name; adulterated = filthy, decomposed or harmful contents; misbranded = false or misleading labelling.

D&C Act 1940: objectives, definitions an: The Act controls import (Chapter III) and manufacture, sale and distribution (Chapter IV) of drugs and cosmetics
'Drug' includes medicines, devices notified by the Government and substances to diagnose or treat
Patent or proprietary medicines are defined separately
Chapter IV-A covers Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani drugs
Advisory and testing bodies: DTAB: technical advice to the Centre and states
CDL Kolkata: statutory and appellate testing laboratory
Government Analysts test samples drawn by Inspectors
DCGI heads CDSCO and licenses new drugs, imports and clinical trials
Drug Inspectors: qualifications, powers: Inspectors can enter, inspect, take samples, search and seize stock and records
The sample is divided into four portions, sealed and signed
Fair price is paid unless the owner refuses
An Inspector must not disclose information except for official purposes
Misbranded, adulterated and spurious dru: Misbranded: false or misleading label, coloured to hide damage
Adulterated: filthy, decomposed, toxic container, unpermitted colour
Spurious: imitation, substitute, or false manufacturer name
Making or selling adulterated or spurious drugs can bring long prison terms and fines
Cognisable and non-bailable for serious offences
D&C Rules 1945: manufacturing licences: Separate licences for different categories of drugs (e.g. general, Schedule C/C1, large-volume parenterals)
Loan licence: using another licensee's manufacturing facility
Technical staff must be approved by the licensing authority
Joint inspection before grant or renewal of licences for certain categories
Licence can be suspended or cancelled after a hearing
D&C Rules: sale licences and conditions: Retail licence requires a registered pharmacist
Wholesale licence requires a competent person (qualified or experienced)
Restricted licences for dealers in remote areas
Purchase and sale records kept for the set period
Schedule H sold only on prescription; H1 also needs a separate register
Import of drugs and cosmetics: Import needs a registration certificate for the manufacturer/product and an import licence
Small quantities allowed for personal use, test or analysis
Spurious, adulterated or misbranded drugs cannot be imported
Schedules to the Rules: C and C1: biological and special products (sera, vaccines, insulin)
H: prescription only; H1: certain antibiotics, anti-TB, habit-forming drugs
X: narcotic and psychotropic, stricter records
G: use under medical supervision; J: diseases a drug may not claim to cure; K: exemptions
M: GMP; L-1: GLP; P: life period; S: cosmetic standards; T: Ayurvedic GMP
Labelling and packing: Labels must carry name, strength, batch number, manufacturing and expiry dates, licence number, manufacturer
Schedule H, H1 and X carry specific warning boxes
Parenterals and biologicals have extra labelling rules
Cosmetics labels list ingredients and manufacturer
New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019: A new drug is one not previously approved in India for that use or form
Clinical trial needs CDSCO permission and a registered ethics committee
Compensation is payable for trial-related injury or death
BA/BE studies need approval and registered centres
Medical Devices Rules 2017: Classes A (low), B (low–moderate), C (moderate–high), D (high) risk
A and B licensed by state authority; C and D by the central authority
Manufacturers need a quality management system
Notified bodies audit class A and B manufacturers
Clinical investigation rules apply to new devices
Cosmetics Rules 2020: Import of cosmetics needs registration with CDSCO
Prohibited and restricted ingredients are listed
Labelling must not make drug-like claims
Pharmacy Act, NDPS Act and DMR Act: Pharmacy Act 1948 created the Pharmacy Council of India and state councils
NDPS Act 1985 distinguishes narcotic drugs (from plants like opium, coca, cannabis) and psychotropic substances
DMR Act 1954 bans advertisements claiming cures for listed diseases
Drug pricing and other laws: NPPA (1997) fixes ceiling prices under DPCO 2013
Scheduled formulations are those in the NLEM
Market-based pricing: ceiling from the average price of brands with ≥ 1% market share
MTP Act governs termination of pregnancy

refs.Cleanrooms and contamination control: Revised Schedule M; WHO-GMP sterile products

items: Quality assurance covers the whole system; quality control is the testing part of it; GMP is the part of QA that ensures consistent manufacture.
Cleanroom grades: A is the critical aseptic zone (filling), B is its background, C and D are for less critical steps.
Qualification order: DQ (design) → IQ (installation) → OQ (operation) → PQ (performance).
ALCOA+: Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate, plus Complete, Consistent, Enduring and Available.
ICH Q1 long-term stability for climatic zone IVb (India): 30 °C / 75% RH; accelerated: 40 °C / 75% RH for 6 months.
Clinical trial phases: I (safety, small group), II (efficacy and dose), III (large confirmatory), IV (post-marketing surveillance).
OOS means a test result outside specification; it needs a documented laboratory investigation before any retest.
GLP applies to laboratory studies; GCP to trials in humans; do not swap their scope.

Revised Schedule M: GMP requirements: Revised Schedule M adds a pharmaceutical quality system, quality risk management and product quality reviews
Premises: logical flow, segregation, HVAC suited to the product
Cleanrooms and contamination control: Grade A: aseptic filling (unidirectional airflow); B: background for A; C and D: less critical steps
HEPA filtration and pressure cascades prevent contamination
Environmental monitoring: viable and non-viable particles
WFI must meet tight microbial and endotoxin limits
Documentation: SOPs describe how; records prove it was done
Batch manufacturing records give full traceability
Master formula is the approved recipe
Data integrity failures are a major inspection finding
Validation and qualification: Process validation: design, qualification, continued verification
Cleaning validation sets residue limits between products
Change control, deviations and CAPA: Change control assesses impact before any change
CAPA fixes root causes and prevents recurrence
Recalls are classed by risk to health
Good Laboratory Practices: Schedule L-1 sets GLP for quality control labs
Reference standards stored and used under control
Stability: long-term 30 °C/75% RH for zone IVb; accelerated 40 °C/75% RH
Good Clinical Practice: Phase I: safety in a small group; II: efficacy and dose; III: confirmatory; IV: post-marketing
Informed consent before any trial procedure
Serious adverse events reported within set timelines
ICH quality guidelines overview: Q1 stability, Q2 analytical validation, Q3 impurities
Q8 development, Q9 risk management, Q10 quality system

refs.Tablet coating and evaluation: Lachman: Tablet coating; IP general tests

items: Friability: tumble 100 revolutions (25 rpm for 4 minutes); weight loss should be not more than 1%.
Dissolution apparatus: 1 basket, 2 paddle, 3 reciprocating cylinder, 4 flow-through cell; 5–7 are mainly for transdermal products.
Autoclave: 121 °C for 15 minutes (about 15 psi). Dry heat: 160 °C for 2 hours. Sterilizing filters are 0.22 µm.
Glass: Type I borosilicate (parenterals), Type II treated soda-lime, Type III soda-lime, Type IV (NP) general purpose non-parenteral.
HLB scale: low HLB (3–6) emulsifiers give w/o emulsions; high HLB (8–18) give o/w emulsions.
Capping and lamination usually come from entrapped air, too many fines or worn tooling.
Enteric-coated tablets must resist the acid stage and disintegrate only in buffer.
Flocculated suspensions settle fast but redisperse easily; deflocculated ones settle slowly but form a hard cake.

Preformulation and physical pharmacy: Solubility, pKa, partition coefficient guide formulation
Polymorphs differ in solubility and stability
Flow: angle of repose < 30° is excellent; Carr's index and Hausner ratio
Tablets: excipients and manufacturing: Diluent, binder, disintegrant, lubricant, glidant each have a role
Wet granulation: mix, granulate, dry, size
Capping and lamination: entrapped air, worn tooling
Sticking and picking: moisture or too little lubricant
Tablet coating and evaluation: Film coating is thin and fast; sugar coating is thick and slow
Disintegration: uncoated tablets typically within 15 minutes (IP)
Capsules: Soft gelatin capsules hold liquids and oils
Gelatin plus plasticiser and water make the shell
Liquid orals: Suspensions need suspending and wetting agents
Emulsions: o/w or w/o; HLB of emulsifier decides type
Creaming is reversible; cracking is not
Semisolids and suppositories: Ointment bases: oleaginous, absorption, water-removable, water-soluble
Creams are emulsions; gels are semisolid systems
Suppository bases: cocoa butter (melts) and PEG (dissolves)
Parenteral products: Parenterals must be sterile, pyrogen-free and particle-free
Water for injection and isotonic adjustment
Type I glass for most parenterals
LVP: large volume infusions; SVP: small volume
Lyophilisation for heat- or moisture-sensitive drugs
Sterilization and aseptic processing: Dry heat 160 °C for 2 hours; depyrogenation needs higher temperatures
Membrane filtration 0.22 µm for heat-labile solutions
Biological indicators: Geobacillus stearothermophilus (steam), Bacillus atrophaeus (dry heat, EO)
Ophthalmic and other sterile preparation: Eye drops must be sterile and close to isotonic
Multidose eye drops need a preservative (e.g. benzalkonium chloride)
pH and viscosity affect comfort and contact time
Aerosols and novel drug delivery: Controlled release keeps levels steady and reduces dosing
Packaging: Plastics can leach or absorb drugs
Surgical dressings and pharmacopoeial ca: Surgical dressings and sutures have pharmacopoeial standards
Isotonic: use freezing-point depression or sodium chloride equivalent

Metabolism and excretion: Phase I and phase II reactions
One-compartment model: IV bolus: k, t½, Vd, AUC

items: t½ = 0.693/k. Clearance CL = k × Vd. Vd = dose/C0 for an IV bolus.
AUC = F × dose / CL. Absolute bioavailability F = (AUCoral/AUCiv) × (Doseiv/Doseoral).
Steady state is reached in about 4–5 half-lives whatever the dose.
Loading dose = Css × Vd / F. Maintenance dose rate = Css × CL / F.
Bioequivalence: 90% confidence interval of the test/reference ratio for Cmax and AUC within 80–125%.
Weak acids are better absorbed in acidic pH (unionised); weak bases in alkaline pH.
Zero-order elimination (e.g. ethanol, high-dose phenytoin) removes a constant amount per time, so t½ is not constant.
A large Vd means extensive tissue distribution, not a large plasma volume.

Drug absorption: Most drugs are absorbed by passive diffusion
Food, gastric emptying and formulation alter absorption
Distribution and protein binding: Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration
High protein binding limits free drug
Displacement from binding sites can cause toxicity (e.g. warfarin)
Metabolism and excretion: Inducers speed up metabolism; inhibitors slow it
One-compartment model: IV bolus: C = C0 e^{−kt}; t½ = 0.693/k
Oral: Cmax and tmax depend on ka and k
Multiple dosing and dose adjustment: Maintenance dose rate = Css × CL / F
Renal impairment: reduce dose or lengthen interval for renally cleared drugs
Bioavailability and bioequivalence: Relative bioavailability compares two non-IV products
BE study: crossover design with washout
Acceptance: 90% CI of Cmax and AUC ratios within 80–125%
Non-linear and two-compartment kinetics: At high doses elimination becomes zero order (phenytoin, ethanol)
Small dose increases can cause large concentration rises
Two-compartment: distribution phase then elimination phase

Limit tests and impurities: Limit tests for chloride and sulphate
Limit tests for lead and heavy metals
IR spectroscopy, AAS and flame photometr: IR regions and functional group frequencies
NMR and mass spectrometry basics: Mass spectrometry: ionisation and molecular ion
Biological and microbiological tests: Pyrogen test and bacterial endotoxin (LAL) test

items: Beer–Lambert law: A = ε b c, valid for dilute solutions and monochromatic light.
Karl Fischer reagent: iodine, sulphur dioxide, a base (pyridine or imidazole) and methanol; it determines water content.
Limit tests: chloride uses silver nitrate (turbidity); sulphate uses barium chloride; iron uses thioglycollic acid (purple colour); arsenic uses the Gutzeit apparatus with mercuric chloride paper.
Rf = distance moved by the solute / distance moved by the solvent front; always less than 1.
ICH Q2 parameters: specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, LOD, LOQ, robustness. LOD = 3.3σ/S and LOQ = 10σ/S.
Bacterial endotoxin test uses Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL); the rabbit pyrogen test measures temperature rise.
Non-aqueous titration is used for very weak acids or bases (e.g. perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid for weak bases).
Fluorescence intensity is proportional to concentration only at low concentrations; quenching lowers it.

Basics, errors and method validation: Accuracy: closeness to true value; precision: closeness of repeated results
Systematic errors bias results; random errors scatter them
ICH Q2: specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, LOD, LOQ, robustness
Titrimetric analysis: Non-aqueous: perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid for weak bases
Iodometry uses thiosulphate; iodimetry uses iodine directly
EDTA titrations use metal indicators (Eriochrome black T)
Argentometry: Mohr (chromate), Volhard (back titration), Fajans (adsorption indicators)
Limit tests and impurities: Lead and heavy metals: sulphide or dithizone methods
Arsenic: Gutzeit apparatus, stain on mercuric chloride paper
Gravimetry, moisture and alcohol content: Karl Fischer measures water by iodine–SO₂ reaction
Loss on drying includes all volatiles
UV–Visible spectroscopy, colorimetry and: Bathochromic = red shift; hypsochromic = blue shift
Fluorimetry is more sensitive than UV
Nephelometry measures scattered light; turbidimetry measures transmitted
IR spectroscopy, AAS and flame photometr: IR: functional group region 4000–1500 cm⁻¹, fingerprint below 1500
AAS measures metals by absorption at element-specific wavelengths
Flame photometry for Na, K, Li, Ca
Chromatography: Rf = solute distance / solvent front distance
System suitability: resolution, tailing, plate count, repeatability
GC needs volatile, thermally stable samples
NMR and mass spectrometry basics: NMR chemical shift in ppm from TMS
Mass spectrometry gives molecular ion and fragments
Electrochemical methods: Potentiometry measures EMF; glass electrode for pH
Polarography uses a dropping mercury electrode
Biological and microbiological tests: Sterility test: membrane filtration or direct inoculation, 14 days incubation
Pyrogen test in rabbits; BET uses LAL reagent
Microbial limit tests for non-sterile products

chem.book: Foye: Principles of Medicinal Chemistry; Wilson & Gisvold
topics: Drug design basics and metabolism chemistry
Antitubercular, antimalarial, antiviral and antifungal drugs

Drug design basics and metabolism chemis: Chemistry of phase I and II metabolism
Diuretics and antidiabetics: Oral antidiabetics: sulphonylureas, biguanides, DPP-4 and SGLT2 inhibitors

items: The β-lactam ring is essential for penicillin and cephalosporin action; penicillinase-resistant penicillins include methicillin and cloxacillin.
Common prodrugs: enalapril → enalaprilat, levodopa → dopamine, valacyclovir → acyclovir, codeine → morphine.
Benzodiazepines act at the GABA-A receptor; flumazenil reverses them.
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; ACE inhibitors can cause dry cough (bradykinin).
First-line anti-TB drugs: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (and streptomycin).
Vitamin chemical names: B1 thiamine, B2 riboflavin, B3 niacin, B6 pyridoxine, B12 cyanocobalamin, C ascorbic acid, K phylloquinone.
Metformin is a biguanide (no hypoglycaemia alone); sulphonylureas cause hypoglycaemia.
Know the class of each named drug: questions give a drug and ask its class or mechanism.

Drug design basics and metabolism chemis: Bioisosteres replace groups with similar properties
Metabolism usually makes drugs more polar for excretion
CNS drugs: Benzodiazepines act on GABA-A; antagonist flumazenil
Autonomic drugs: Adrenaline: α and β agonist; salbutamol: β2 selective
Propranolol: non-selective β blocker; atenolol: β1 selective
Cardiovascular drugs: ACE inhibitors end in -pril; ARBs in -sartan
Diuretics and antidiabetics: Loop diuretics (furosemide) are the most potent
Thiazides act on the distal tubule
Gliptins inhibit DPP-4; gliflozins inhibit SGLT2
Antihistamines, steroids and hormones: H1 blockers: first generation sedate (chlorpheniramine), second do not (cetirizine)
Antibiotics: Penicillins and cephalosporins inhibit cell wall synthesis
Aminoglycosides act on the 30S ribosome; ototoxic and nephrotoxic
Sulphonamides with trimethoprim block folate synthesis
Antitubercular, antimalarial, antiviral: First-line TB drugs: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
Acyclovir for herpes; tenofovir and others for HIV
Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis; amphotericin B binds ergosterol
Anticancer drugs: Vinca alkaloids and taxanes act on microtubules
Imatinib is a targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor
Vitamins: B1 thiamine (beriberi), B3 niacin (pellagra), B12 (pernicious anaemia)

pcol.book: K.D. Tripathi: Essentials of Medical Pharmacology

Experimental pharmacology and biostatist: Probability and tests of significance basics

items: Therapeutic index = LD50 / ED50; a narrow index (digoxin, lithium, warfarin) needs monitoring.
Antidotes: paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine; opioids → naloxone; organophosphates → atropine + pralidoxime; benzodiazepines → flumazenil; heparin → protamine; warfarin → vitamin K.
More antidotes: methanol → fomepizole or ethanol; iron → desferrioxamine; lead → calcium disodium EDTA; digoxin → digoxin-specific Fab fragments.
Enzyme inducers: rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone. Inhibitors: ketoconazole, erythromycin, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin.
Known teratogens: thalidomide, isotretinoin, warfarin, valproate, ACE inhibitors (2nd–3rd trimester).
PvPI was launched in 2010; its National Coordination Centre is at the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.
Potency is the dose needed; efficacy is the maximum effect. A more potent drug is not necessarily more effective.
Type A ADRs are dose-related and predictable; Type B are bizarre and unpredictable (e.g. allergy).

General pharmacology: Tolerance needs higher doses for the same effect
Autonomic nervous system: Muscarinic agonists slow the heart and constrict pupils
α1: vasoconstriction; β1: heart; β2: bronchodilation
Central nervous system: Barbiturates are more dangerous in overdose than benzodiazepines
Opioids cause respiratory depression and miosis
Cardiovascular and renal drugs: First-line antihypertensives: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, CCBs, thiazides
Heart failure: ACE inhibitors, β blockers, diuretics
Amiodarone: broad antiarrhythmic with many side effects
Blood, respiratory and GI drugs: Heparin acts fast (antithrombin); warfarin slowly (vitamin K antagonist)
Salbutamol relieves asthma; inhaled steroids prevent attacks
Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) reduce acid most
Endocrine pharmacology: Insulin types: rapid, short, intermediate, long acting
Hypoglycaemia is the main risk of insulin and sulphonylureas
Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal axis
Autacoids and NSAIDs: Prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa; NSAIDs remove this
Antimicrobial chemotherapy: Resistance by enzymes (β-lactamase), efflux, target change
Adverse drug reactions and pharmacovigil: Type A: dose-related; Type B: unpredictable
Enzyme inhibitors raise levels of other drugs
ADR reporting form available to all health workers
Toxicology and antidotes: First aid, decontamination, supportive care, then antidote
Iron: desferrioxamine; lead: EDTA; methanol: fomepizole or ethanol
Experimental pharmacology and biostatist: Bioassay compares test and standard responses
Acute, sub-acute and chronic toxicity studies

bio.n: Blood products, vaccines, sera and biotech
bio.book: Ananthanarayan: Microbiology; D&C Rules Part X-B and Schedule F; NACO blood bank standards

refs.Blood collection and testing: D&C Rules Part X-B; NACO standards

items: Mandatory screening of donated blood in India: HIV 1 & 2, hepatitis B (HBsAg), hepatitis C, syphilis and malaria.
Whole blood in CPDA-1 keeps about 35 days at 2–6 °C; red cells in SAGM about 42 days; platelets about 5 days at 20–24 °C with continuous agitation.
Most vaccines are stored at 2–8 °C; freezing damages adsorbed vaccines (DPT, TT, hepatitis B), which the shake test detects.
Live attenuated: BCG, OPV, MMR. Inactivated: IPV, rabies. Toxoids: tetanus, diphtheria. Recombinant: hepatitis B.
Monoclonal antibody names end in -mab; biosimilars need comparability studies against the reference product.
The vaccine vial monitor shows cumulative heat exposure, not freezing.
Cryoprecipitate is rich in factor VIII and fibrinogen.

Microbiology basics, sterilization and d: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan; Gram-negative: outer membrane
Autoclave sterilises; boiling does not kill spores
Blood collection and testing: Donors: healthy, age and weight limits, haemoglobin above minimum
Mandatory tests: HIV 1 & 2, HBsAg, HCV, syphilis, malaria
ABO and Rh grouping and cross-match
Blood components and plasma products: Red cells in SAGM about 42 days
Platelets about 5 days at 20–24 °C with agitation
Fresh frozen plasma stored frozen, about 1 year
Vaccines: types and production: Conjugate vaccines (Hib, pneumococcal) work in infants
Cold chain and vaccine handling: Freezing damages adsorbed vaccines (DPT, TT, hepatitis B)
Use open vials as per the multi-dose vial policy
Sera, antitoxins and immunoglobulins: IgG crosses the placenta; IgM appears first
Passive immunity is immediate but short-lived
Biotech products: rDNA: gene inserted into a vector, expressed in host cells
Biosimilars need comparability with the reference product

topics: Evaluation and adulteration of crude drugs

Evaluation and adulteration of crude dru: Organoleptic, microscopic, physical and chemical evaluation
Herbal drugs and standardisation: Brahmi, tulsi, bael and other Indian herbs

items: Rauwolfia serpentina root → reserpine; Cinchona bark → quinine; Belladonna leaf → atropine and hyoscyamine.
Nux vomica seed → strychnine and brucine; Opium latex → morphine, codeine, papaverine; Ipecac root → emetine.
Digitalis leaf → digitoxin (cardiac glycoside); Senna leaf and aloe → anthraquinone glycosides (laxative).
Tests: Dragendorff for alkaloids; Vitali–Morin for tropane alkaloids; Keller–Killiani for cardiac glycosides; Borntrager for anthraquinones; Thalleioquin for quinine.
Learn the part of the plant used (root, bark, leaf, seed): it is a common question.
Do not mix Vitali–Morin (tropane alkaloids) with Keller–Killiani (deoxy sugars of cardiac glycosides).

Introduction, cultivation and collection: Crude drugs classified alphabetically, taxonomically, morphologically, chemically or pharmacologically
Store away from light and moisture
Evaluation and adulteration of crude dru: Adulteration: substitution, inferior grade, exhausted drug
Glycoside-containing drugs: Keller–Killiani for cardiac glycosides; Borntrager for anthraquinones
Tannins, volatile oils and resins: Tannins precipitate proteins; test with ferric chloride
Herbal drugs and standardisation: Brahmi for memory; tulsi as adaptogen; bael for diarrhoea
Standardise herbal products by marker compounds
WHO guidelines for quality of herbal medicines

hosp.n: Hospital and clinical pharmacy, anatomy and physiology

topics: Anatomy and physiology: blood, cardiovascular and respiratory

items: ABC analysis ranks items by annual value (A: few items, most value); VED ranks by criticality (vital, essential, desirable).
Drugs needing therapeutic drug monitoring: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, theophylline.
The Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee selects drugs for the hospital formulary and reviews drug use.
Normal adult values: blood pressure about 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 60–100/min, haemoglobin about 13–17 g/dL (men) and 12–15 g/dL (women).
Unit-dose distribution reduces medication errors compared with floor stock.
Insulin comes from pancreatic β-cells, glucagon from α-cells.

Hospital pharmacy organisation: Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee selects formulary drugs
Formulary lists approved drugs for the hospital
Hospital pharmacist heads purchase, storage and distribution
Purchase, storage and inventory: Cold chain for vaccines, insulin, biologicals
Clinical pharmacy: Read prescriptions carefully; check dose, route, interactions
Counsel on dose, timing, side effects
TDM for narrow therapeutic index drugs
Anatomy and physiology: blood, cardiovas: Heart pumps through pulmonary and systemic circulation
Anatomy and physiology: nervous, endocri: Neurons send impulses; synapses use neurotransmitters
Nephron filters blood and forms urine
Digestion and absorption mostly in the small intestine
Health education and public health: Communicable diseases spread by air, water, vectors or contact
National health programmes: immunisation, TB, malaria, HIV

inv.book: CDSCO guidance documents; D&C Act enforcement chapters

Sampling, seizure and legal procedure: Sending samples to the Government Analyst
Investigating spurious and NSQ drugs: Coordination with state regulators and police

items: An Inspector's statutory sample is divided into four portions, sealed and marked; one goes to the Government Analyst.
